SASA 2026 Workshop: Interpretable Machine Learning (IML)

Solution

Marvin N. Wright

November 2026

Setup and data preparation

We use data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2017–March 2020 to predict HbA1c (glycohemoglobin) from age, gender, ancestry, BMI, glucose, eGFR, cholesterol and smoking in adults. The file nhanes_hba1c.csv was created from the public NHANES data with the script data_prep.R.

# load data
dat = read.csv("nhanes_hba1c.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)

# convert integer variables to numeric
dat[] = lapply(dat, function(x) if (is.integer(x)) as.numeric(x) else x)

# define outcome variable
var.outcome = "glycohemoglobin"

# define two data sets for training and external validation based on sequential 
# ID, then remove the ID (it is not a feature)
ind_train = which(dat$SEQN < 120000)
dat$SEQN = NULL
dat_train = dat[ind_train, ]
dat_val = dat[-ind_train, ]

Fit a prediction model

Now fit a prediction model, e.g., a random forest with the ranger package.

library(ranger)
model = ranger(
  x = dat_train[, !(colnames(dat_train) == var.outcome)],
  y = dat_train[, var.outcome]
)

Check the performance, is it OK? We don’t want to explain a bad model.

pred = predict(model, data = dat_val)$predictions
obs = dat_val[, var.outcome]
sqrt(mean((pred-obs)^2)) # RMSE
## [1] 0.6338382

Feature effects

We start with feature effects. They are implemented in the iml package. For help, see the package website. Create a partial dependence plot (PDP), individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots, and an accumulated local effects (ALE) plot for the feature “age”. How to interpret it? Do you find any other interesting features?

💡 Hint 1: First create a Predictor object that wraps the model and the data.
💡 Hint 2: Then call FeatureEffect$new(...) and plot(...) on the result. 
library(iml)
# Create a Predictor object
predictor = Predictor$new(
  model = model, 
  data = dat_train[, !(colnames(dat_train) == var.outcome)], 
  y = dat_train[, var.outcome]
)
# Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) 
eff = FeatureEffect$new(predictor, feature = "age", method = "pdp")
plot(eff)

# Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) + PDP
eff = FeatureEffect$new(predictor, feature = "age", method = "pdp+ice")
plot(eff)

# Accumulated Local Effects (ALE)
eff = FeatureEffect$new(predictor, feature = "age", method = "ale")
plot(eff)

Feature importance

Now, let’s try feature importance. For permutation feature importance, we can use the iml package again. We can also re-use the Predictor object we created above. Plot PFI for all features (in one plot). Which are the most important features for the model?

💡 Hint: The syntax is similar to feature effects. Call FeatureImp$new(...) and plot(...) on the result. 
# Permutation feature importance (PFI)
imp = FeatureImp$new(predictor, loss = "rmse", compare = "difference")
plot(imp)

Conditional feature importance is not available in the iml package. We can use the cpi package instead. It uses the mlr3 package for machine learning, which makes it a little bit more complex if you have not used it before. For help, see the package website. Since our dataset has mixed continuous and categorical features, we have to use the seqknockoff package to generate knockoff variables. This package is only available from Github, so you have to install it first using the command devtools::install_github("kormama1/seqknockoff").

⚠️ This is a rather difficult exercise. Feel free to skip it if you have no experience with mlr3. ⚠️

💡 Hint 1: First create a regression task with mlr3 from our data.
💡 Hint 2: Then run cpi(...) on the task. Look at the examples in the cpi help. 
library(cpi)
# devtools::install_github("kormama1/seqknockoff")
library(seqknockoff)
library(mlr3verse)

mytask = as_task_regr(dat_train, target = var.outcome)
imp_cpi = cpi(task = mytask, learner = lrn("regr.ranger"), 
              resampling = rsmp("holdout"), 
              knockoff_fun = seqknockoff::knockoffs_seq)

Now plot the results, e.g., using ggplot2. Are the results different than those from PFI? Which features differ and why?

ggplot(data.frame(feature = imp_cpi$Variable, importance = imp_cpi$CPI), 
       aes(x = reorder(feature, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + 
  coord_flip() + 
  xlab("Feature")

For LOCO (Leave-One-Covariate-Out), let’s try to implement it manually. Do you remember the algorithm?

💡 Hint: First, fit a full model with all features. Then, for each feature, fit a new model without this feature and calculate the increase in RMSE on the validation data. 
feature_names = colnames(dat_train)[colnames(dat_train) != var.outcome]
imp_loco = sapply(feature_names, function(var){
  model_loco = ranger(
    x = dat_train[, !(colnames(dat_train) %in% c(var.outcome, var))],
    y = dat_train[, var.outcome]
  )
  pred_loco = predict(model_loco, data = dat_val)$predictions
  sqrt(mean((pred_loco - obs)^2)) - sqrt(mean((pred - obs)^2)) # RMSE
})

Now plot the results. Are the results different than those from PFI and CFI?

ggplot(data.frame(feature = feature_names, importance = imp_loco), 
       aes(x = reorder(feature, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + 
  coord_flip() + 
  xlab("Feature")

Shapley values

There are several packages for Shapley values. Here, we use the fastshap package. For help, see the package website. For visualization, we recommend the shapviz package; package website.

First, calculate SHAP values with fastshap.

💡 Hint 1: This time, we need a prediction wrapper function that takes the model and new data as input and returns the predictions.
💡 Hint 2: The prediction wrapper for ranger could look like this: pfun = function(object, newdata) { predict(object, data = newdata)$predictions }
💡 Hint 3: Call fastshap::explain(...) on the model, training data, and prediction wrapper function.
💡 Hint 4: Use adjust = TRUE (requires nsim > 1, e.g. nsim = 10) so that the SHAP values of each observation sum up to its prediction minus the average prediction. This also sets the baseline needed for the plots. 
library(fastshap)

pfun = function(object, newdata) {
  predict(object, data = newdata)$predictions
}
fs = fastshap::explain(object = model, 
                       X = dat_train[, !(colnames(dat_train) == var.outcome)], 
                       pred_wrapper = pfun, nsim = 10, adjust = TRUE)

Then create a shapviz object for visualization.

💡 Hint: Call shapviz(...) on the SHAP values and training data. 
library(shapviz)
fsv = shapviz(fs, X = dat_train[, !(colnames(dat_train) == var.outcome)])

Now create some plots. They are all functions starting with sv_.... Try importance, beeswarm/summary and dependence (as you know from the lecture). You can also try local explanations with waterfall and force.

💡 Hint 1: The beeswarm plot is also implemented in sv_importance (argument kind = "beeswarm").
💡 Hint 2: Dependence plots can be colored with argument color_var.
💡 Hint 3: For local explanations, you need to specify a row index (e.g., 1 or 2) to be explained. 
# Importance plot
sv_importance(fsv)

# Beeswarm / summary plot
sv_importance(fsv, kind = "beeswarm")

# Dependence plot
sv_dependence(fsv, "age", color_var = NULL)

# Colored dependence plot
sv_dependence(fsv, "age", color_var = "gender")

# Waterfall plot
sv_waterfall(fsv, 1)

# Force plot
sv_force(fsv, 2)
